sources.title: NGSS MS-LS1-8: Gather and synthesize information that sensory receptors respond to stimuli by sending messages to the brain for immediate behavior or storage as memories
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 14.3 Motor Responses
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 14.1 Sensory Perception
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 12.1 Basic Structure and Function of the Nervous System

note.text: Your skin has sensory receptors. Some respond to heat or pain.

steps.title: Stimulus
steps.instruction: Trace the flame under the hand.

note.text: A stimulus is a change a receptor can detect, like the heat of a hot stove.

steps.title: Spinal cord
steps.instruction: Trace the spinal cord, cut across.

note.text: This is a slice across the spinal cord. Signals from the body enter it through nerves.
The butterfly-shaped gray matter is where neurons connect to each other.

steps.title: Sensory neuron
steps.instruction: Draw the signal from the hand to the spinal cord.

note.text: Receptors start a signal. A sensory neuron carries it from the skin to the spinal cord.
note.remember: Sensory neuron: body to spinal cord.

steps.title: Interneuron
steps.instruction: Draw the short neuron inside the spinal cord.

note.text: In the spinal cord, the signal passes to another neuron, which connects straight to a motor neuron.

steps.title: Motor neuron
steps.instruction: Draw the signal back out to the arm muscle.

note.text: A motor neuron carries the command out to a muscle.
note.remember: Motor neuron: spinal cord to muscle.

note.text: The biceps contracts and pulls your hand away. This fast, automatic response is a reflex.

steps.title: Message to the brain
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow going up to the brain.

note.text: Signals also travel up to the brain. You feel the pain, and you can remember not to touch the stove again.

steps.title: The reflex arc
steps.why: The signal goes in on a sensory neuron, connects in the spinal cord and comes back out on a motor neuron.
steps.hint: It starts in the skin and ends at a muscle.

steps.title: Why so fast?
steps.question: Why can you pull your hand away before you even feel the pain?

options.text: The signal turns around in the spinal cord, without waiting for the brain
options.feedback: Yes. The short path is fast, so less damage is done. The brain gets the message a moment later.
Muscles don't sense heat. Receptors in the skin do, and nerves carry the signal.
The brain isn't in the loop. The signal connects in the spinal cord.
Something has to signal the muscle: a motor neuron from the spinal cord.

steps.title: Memory
steps.instruction: Think about the arrow up to the brain.
steps.question: What does the signal that reaches the brain let you do?

options.text: Feel the pain and remember to avoid the stove next time
options.feedback: Right. Messages to the brain can lead to action now or be stored as memories.
The spinal cord already did that. The brain lets you feel it and remember.
The brain does get the message. That's how you feel the pain.
Your body can't change the stove. The brain lets you learn to avoid it.
